title: What is REST, and what makes an API "RESTful" rather than just "an API over HTTP"?
tldr: Full REST requires HATEOAS-driven hypermedia, not just HTTP verbs + JSON — most production 'REST' APIs are a pragmatic subset that skips it.

title: Why is statelessness a core REST constraint, and what breaks if you violate it?
tldr: Statelessness means every request is self-contained, enabling free load-balancing and clean failover — violating it forces sticky sessions.

title: What's the difference between a "safe" and an "idempotent" HTTP method, and why does it matter for retries and caches?
tldr: Safe = read-only; idempotent = repeating it has the same end state — idempotent requests are safe to auto-retry, POST/PATCH by default are neither.

title: Walk through PUT vs PATCH vs POST for updating a resource — when would you use each?
tldr: PUT replaces the whole resource, PATCH applies a partial change, POST is for creation or non-idempotent actions — mixing up PUT with a partial body silently nulls fields.

title: When do you return 400 vs 422, and 401 vs 403?
tldr: 400 is malformed syntax, 422 is well-formed but business-invalid; 401 means unauthenticated, 403 means authenticated but not permitted.

title: A client's POST to create a payment times out — they don't know if it succeeded. How do you make this safe to retry?
tldr: An idempotency key lets the server cache and replay the first response to a retried POST, making non-idempotent operations like payments safe to retry.

title: What are the main API versioning strategies, and what are the trade-offs?
tldr: URI versioning is simple but leaks into every path, header/content-negotiation versioning is purer but less discoverable — additive, backward-compatible changes avoid needing a bump at all.

title: Offset-based vs. cursor-based pagination — how do they work, and why does it matter at scale?
tldr: Offset pagination scans and discards skipped rows, getting slower and less stable at depth; cursor pagination anchors to an indexed value and stays fast and stable regardless of depth.

title: How does rate limiting actually work under the hood — walk through the token bucket algorithm?
tldr: A token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity while enforcing a steady refill rate, avoiding the boundary-burst flaw of a naive fixed-window counter.

title: Explain HTTP caching: Cache-Control, ETag/If-None-Match, and when a 304 gets returned.
tldr: Cache-Control governs storability/freshness, ETag + If-None-Match let the server issue a bodyless 304 when the cached copy is still valid.

title: What is CORS, why does the browser enforce it, and what triggers a preflight request?
tldr: CORS lets a server opt specific origins into cross-origin access; the browser preflights any 'non-simple' request (non-GET/HEAD/POST, custom headers, or an unusual Content-Type) with an OPTIONS check first.

title: Walk through the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, and explain when you'd use client credentials instead.
tldr: Authorization code flow keeps the access token off the browser via a back-channel exchange, for use whenever a human user grants access; client credentials skips the user entirely for service-to-service calls.

title: What is HATEOAS, and why does Roy Fielding say most "REST APIs" aren't actually REST?
tldr: HATEOAS means clients navigate via links returned in responses instead of hardcoded URIs — without it, Fielding considers an API 'HTTP RPC,' not true REST.

title: Production users report an API endpoint is "slow." Walk through how you'd diagnose it.
tldr: Diagnosing 'slow' starts with p95/p99 latency and distributed tracing to isolate which layer (DB, downstream call, app code) is actually responsible, then fix and re-measure against the same metrics.

title: What's a "chatty" API, and how does it relate to the N+1 problem?
tldr: A chatty/N+1 API pays one round trip per related item instead of batching them — fixed with bulk endpoints, embedding, or a query language that lets the client shape one request.

title: Why do persistent (keep-alive) connections matter for API performance, and what's actually happening at the TCP/HTTP layer?
tldr: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses a TCP connection across requests to avoid repeated handshake cost; HTTP/2 goes further by multiplexing multiple requests over one connection at once.

title: Compare gRPC and REST — when would you choose gRPC for an API?
tldr: gRPC trades REST's human-debuggable JSON and browser-native accessibility for binary protobuf, native streaming, and strong typing — best for internal service-to-service calls, not public APIs.

title: Compare GraphQL and REST — what real problem does GraphQL solve?
tldr: GraphQL lets the client specify exactly the fields/shape it needs in one request, solving REST's over-fetching and under-fetching — at the cost of new caching and query-cost risks.

title: A downstream API your service depends on starts failing intermittently — how does the circuit breaker pattern help, and how is it different from just retrying?
tldr: Retry handles transient blips; a circuit breaker trips open after sustained failures to fail fast and protect both caller and callee from cascading overload, then half-opens to probe recovery.

title: What is backpressure, and why does it matter when one API/service produces data faster than a downstream consumer can process it?
tldr: Backpressure lets a slow consumer signal capacity back to a fast producer so it throttles instead of overwhelming buffers — without it, unhandled producers must be dropped, buffered, or errored on the consumer side.
